write.modelAfterSubmit:
In many Vietnamese schools, a student's final mark depends mainly on written tests. Some people argue that projects should play a bigger role. I largely agree, because projects show what students can do over time, but written tests should still be part of the mark.

What makes projects valuable is that they reward steady work rather than a single performance. A student who builds a model bridge over several weeks has to research, test ideas and correct mistakes, which reinforces learning far more than cramming the night before an exam. Moreover, a project cannot be ruined by one bad day, so it gives a fairer picture of a student's ability.

Admittedly, critics point out that projects are harder to mark fairly, since some students receive help from parents or tutors. This is a real problem. However, it is a reason to design projects carefully, not to rely only on tests. Teachers can ask students to present their work and answer questions about it, which only students who truly understand their project can do well. A short written test can then check the basic knowledge that every student needs.

In conclusion, projects should count for more than they do now, while tests remain a useful check. Only by combining the two can schools reward both understanding and effort.
